name: Fadogia agrestis

lead: Fadogia agrestis is an African plant whose stem extract is sold as a testosterone and libido supplement, usually alongside tongkat ali. It became widely known through podcasts and fitness social media, and people take it for better training, recovery and a more muscular, leaner look.

The chain is a claimed testosterone rise leading to better training and recovery. The research is almost entirely in rats, including a 2005 study reporting higher serum testosterone and more mating behaviour; no human clinical trial was found.

paras: It is taken as a capsule or powder, typically in a stack with tongkat ali, over weeks to months alongside training. Because there are no human trials, results come from user reports.

Rat studies have looked at testicular function and liver and kidney toxicity, and related plant species cause cardiac toxicity in livestock. Human safety data do not exist, and a 2019 analysis found supplement contents differ widely.

angle.text: Fadogia agrestis is a stem extract, often stacked with tongkat ali, taken to raise testosterone for better training, muscle and libido. The idea is a testosterone rise leading to a more muscular, leaner look. Support comes from rat studies; no human trial was found.

lead: Fadogia agrestis (now often classified as Vangueria agrestis) is a plant of the coffee family, Rubiaceae, native to tropical Africa. Its stem has been used in traditional African medicine as an aphrodisiac and for pain and inflammation, and extracts are sold as dietary supplements marketed for testosterone and libido.[1][2][3]

Its appeal for appearance runs through a chain people describe in forums: higher testosterone, to better libido, energy and training drive, to more muscle and a leaner, more masculine physique. Some users also take it when trying to regain testicular size or hormonal function after other hormone use.[4][5][6][7]

The research is almost entirely in rodents. A 2005 study in male rats reported higher serum testosterone and more sexual behaviour after dosing with an aqueous stem extract, and a 2023 rat study reported effects on erectile-dysfunction biomarkers.[2][8] Rat studies have also examined testicular function and liver and kidney toxicity.[9][10] No human clinical trial of Fadogia agrestis has been found.

In forums and on podcasts it is often combined with tongkat ali in 'natural testosterone' stacks, and the combination is discussed alongside concerns drawn from the animal toxicity studies.[4][11] In the United States, supplements are sold under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act framework, under which the FDA does not approve supplements for safety or effectiveness before sale.[12]
infobox: Tropical Africa (the genus ranges from West to East and southern Africa)[1]
Sold as a dietary supplement; no drug approval[12]

paras: Fadogia is a genus of more than 100 perennial herbs, subshrubs and shrubs in the family Rubiaceae, found in savanna and woodland across tropical and southern Africa. Fadogia agrestis has been transferred by some taxonomists to Vangueria, which is how it appears in some chemical literature.[1][13] Phytochemical work has identified alkaloids and saponins in stem extracts, and separate studies isolated monoterpene glycosides and ursane-type triterpenoid glycosides, benzophenone glycosides and an iridoid glucoside from the plant.[2][13][14]

Wikipedia describes Fadogia as a genus in the coffee family Rubiaceae, tribe Vanguerieae, of roughly 40 listed species distributed across tropical Africa, with the widest-ranging species stretching from Guinea to the Transvaal; Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia, Tanzania and the Central African Republic hold the most species. F. agrestis is not on that list, consistent with its reassignment by some taxonomists to Vangueria.[15][1] Chemical work on the plant has isolated monoterpene glycosides and ursane-type triterpenoid, benzophenone and iridoid glycosides, studied in laboratory assays for anti-infective activity.[13][14]

People take Fadogia agrestis because of its reputation as a testosterone-supporting herb. The chain they have in mind runs from higher testosterone, to better libido, energy and training capacity, to more muscle and a leaner, more masculine physique, and some users also take it when trying to regain testicular size or hormonal function after other hormone use.[4][5][6][7] The direct evidence for the first link is a 2005 rat study; no human trial has measured testosterone, muscle or appearance with Fadogia agrestis.[2]

Traditionally, Fadogia agrestis is described as being used in African medicine for its analgesic, anti-inflammatory and aphrodisiac activities.[3] Today, supplements claiming to contain it are sold for testosterone support and libido. A 2019 analytical study of 17 dietary supplements claiming to contain F. agrestis found that 12 contained measurable phenolic compounds at low levels and 5 did not, indicating variability in products.[3]

Grokipedia reports that Hausa communities in Nigeria use the stems and roots as an aphrodisiac, and lists further traditional uses for fever, diarrhoea, toothache and urinary complaints across West and East Africa; this account is secondary and its own sourcing is mixed.[1] The 2019 analytical paper opens by describing the plant's use in traditional African medicine as an analgesic and for anti-inflammatory and aphrodisiac activities.[3] A 2012 survey of Ghana's herbal markets, which lists aphrodisiacs among the main uses of traded plants, shows the wider context of such plants in West African commerce.[16]

Taxonomy has moved. Some authorities place the species in Vangueria rather than Fadogia, and the genus is described in Wikipedia as having tribe-level placement in Vanguerieae.[15][1] Grokipedia states the genus was described by Schweinfurth in 1868 and that the species is predicted not to be threatened globally.[1]

Products are sold as oral capsules or extracts, usually of stem or root material, often in blends with tongkat ali and other 'testosterone support' ingredients.[4][11] Under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act, products are treated as food rather than drugs, labels carrying structure/function claims must state that the FDA has not evaluated them, and the agency does not approve supplements for safety or effectiveness before sale.[12]

Content varies. The 2019 analysis of 17 products labelled as containing F. agrestis detected the plant's phenolic compounds in 12 and none in 5.[3] Grokipedia likewise describes the market as unregulated and variably standardised.[1]

sections.h: Tongkat ali and the stacking culture
paras: Fadogia is most often discussed beside tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia), a Southeast Asian root. Wikipedia reports that bodybuilders believe tongkat ali raises testosterone and performance, that clinical evidence is limited, and that side effects reported include nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea and headaches, with rare liver injury mostly in bodybuilders.[17] It also records FDA action in 2006 against seven products marketed on the plant that contained prescription drugs or analogues, and recalls of two coffee brands in 2017 for hidden erectile-dysfunction drug ingredients, illustrating quality questions around the category generally.[17]
On T Nation, posters describe the two herbs as a pair for 'energy and libido', as add-ons to testosterone 'restart' routines, or as a try-first option before other interventions.[4][11][5][18]

subs.h: Animal studies of testosterone and sexual behaviour
paras: In the 2005 study, male albino rats were given an aqueous stem extract at 18, 50 and 100 mg/kg for several days; all doses increased mount and intromission frequency, prolonged ejaculatory latency and increased serum testosterone, with the authors suggesting the testosterone rise might underlie the aphrodisiac effect.[2] A 2023 study in paroxetine-treated rats found that the extract raised nitric oxide, cGMP and antioxidant enzymes and lowered PDE5 and other markers in penile and testicular tissue, in a pattern the authors compared to sildenafil.[8]

Authors of the 2005 rat study framed Fadogia agrestis as a candidate aphrodisiac and suggested the testosterone rise might explain the behavioural effect; the 2008 and 2009 toxicology papers appeared afterwards, examining testicular function indices, liver and kidney cellular effects in rats.[2][9][10] Neither research line has been extended to human participants in published trials.

A 2008 study examined testicular function indices in male rats given the aqueous stem extract and followed recovery for ten days.[9] A 2009 study examined the mode of cellular toxicity of the extract in rat liver and kidney.[10] The abstracts available to this wiki do not report full results, and no regulatory body safety assessment was found.

Separately, other species in the genus and related genera, including Fadogia homblei, Pavetta and Vangueria, are associated with gousiekte, a fatal cardiotoxicosis of ruminants in South Africa; this is a veterinary phenomenon of different plants and has not been shown to apply to supplement use in humans.[19][1]

The 2009 liver and kidney paper and the 2008 testicular paper used the same three extract doses as the 2005 aphrodisiac study (18, 50 and 100 mg/kg), so the doses that raised testosterone in rats were also the ones examined for organ effects.[2][9][10] Grokipedia summarises the toxicology literature as reporting elevated liver markers and testicular changes in rats after repeated dosing, a high acute LD50 for root extract, and no published human poisoning series; it also notes that no new human clinical trials had appeared as of November 2025.[1]

Chemical studies have isolated six monoterpene glycosides from the plant (2008) and, from roots of Vangueria agrestis, four ursane-type triterpenoid glycosides, two benzophenone glycosides and one iridoid glucoside (2020); two of the compounds inhibited Trypanosoma brucei in laboratory assays.[14][13] These papers characterise constituents and anti-infective activity rather than testosterone effects.

Fadogia agrestis became widely known through podcasts and social media as a testosterone-support supplement, usually paired with tongkat ali. On T Nation, users describe taking it with tongkat ali for energy and libido, adding it to 'HPTA restart' and post-cycle routines, or trying it after concerns about testicular size; one poster credits a podcaster's recommendation as 'right', while another reported that SHBG did not change after trying boron, Fadogia and tongkat ali.[4][11][5][18]
Users commonly describe cycling the supplement on and off; this wiki does not give dosing or cycling instructions.

Fadogia agrestis is sold as an oral extract or capsule, and the 2019 analysis of 17 products found measurable phenolic compounds in 12 and none in 5, so product content varies by brand.[3] Podcasts and social media brought it from traditional African use into the Western supplement market, usually alongside tongkat ali.[4][11]

Wikipedia's page on Fadogia treats the genus botanically and does not discuss supplement use, so the supplement's profile rests on podcasts, social media and forums rather than on encyclopedic or clinical coverage.[15] The cultural pattern matches other herbal 'natural testosterone' ingredients: animal studies supply the mechanism claims, and forums supply the human anecdotes, including reports of no measurable change.[2][4][11]

No studies found. Research is limited to rodent studies of aphrodisiac effects, testicular function and organ toxicity,[2][8][9][10] chemical analyses of the plant and supplements,[3][13][14] and veterinary literature on related plants.[19]

lore.intro: Fadogia agrestis is discussed on T Nation as one half of a tongkat ali plus Fadogia 'natural test' stack, often used when trying to restart or support testosterone, with anecdotes ranging from praise to no measurable change.[4][11][5][18]
